newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Tensions rise ahead of OSCE fact-finding mission.
newsitem.headline: Tensions rise ahead of OSCE fact-finding mission.

text.p: Tensions rose in Serbia on Friday as embattled ruling socialists promised more rallies in support of President Slobodan Milosevic to counter month-long opposition protests against alleged election fraud.

The mounting concerns coincide with the arrival later in the day of a pan-European delegation to investigate the opposition allegations which have sparked a month of street protests across Serbia, including Belgrade.

The delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), led by former Spanish Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez, was expected to meet Milosevic and leaders of the opposition Zajedno coalition.

Milosevic invited the OSCE to send a delegation to Belgrade after 33 days of protests over alleged vote-rigging which overturned opposition victories in 15 of Serbia's biggest towns, including the capital.

The tenacity of the protests, which rallied as many as 200,000 people in Belgrade on Thursday, has infuriated socialist hardliners fearing punishment by Milosevic for having lost the elections and mishandling the crisis.

Belgrade student leaders said they would mobilise their supporters to blockade three bridges over the Sava River to snarl up traffic going into Belgrade with the aim of paralysing the city for 30 minutes on Friday.

The embattled socialists recently resorted to organizing rallies of their own in support of Milosevic, in a move that analysts and diplomats describe as "clutching a straw" but also fear could have negative consequences.

"Unless they (opposition) return to where decisions are made, I shall call a rally of all Serbia in Belgrade," Mihail Kertes, a senior Socialist party (SPS) official, said at a rally in northern town of Backa Palanka on Thursday.
Playing safe, the socialists have so far organized rallies in smaller towns where they have bedrock support but attendance has been poor.
Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic has accused the socialists of trying to provoke a civil war in Serbia.
Diplomats believe the SPS, despite the obedient party apparatus, would find it very hard to put together a sizeable rally in Belgrade to compare with Zajedno protests.
"It could easily be a swan song by the party hacks who drummed up the idea," a western diplomat said.
"But all the same it is dangerous because it is inflaming passions. One can only imagine what would happen if a fight broke out between the two groups," he said.
Milosevic has promised he would not use force to quell the demonstrations and police had kept a low profile throughout.
His close associates have recently struck a moderate tone regarding the opposition.

"We believe that all this should be resolved within the institutions of the system," Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic, who is also one of Milosevic's closest personal friends, told a news conference on Thursday.
There were fresh signs of Friday that Milosevic was distancing himself from his hardline party subordinates.
"You cannot hide any longer behind my name," the Belgrade newspaper Dnevni Telegraf, close to government circles, quoted Milosevic as telling his party officials.

"Milosevic is now waiting to see how things work out with the opposition protests, SPS rallies and, naturally, for the verdict of the OSCE mission which he could decide to accept as a face-saving step if all else fails," the diplomat said.
The United States, which has spearheaded pressure for more democracy in Serbia, hopes the OSCE ruling will be binding.

But Milutinovic warned the government would need to consider the OSCE recommendations and Zajedno leaders also said they will not give up their demand to have their victory restored no matter what the OSCE ruling is.
